summary: Anchor on what cannot move (walls, sofa, timber, light). Build a 60/30/10 palette, pick a harmony that suits the style, keep undertones compatible, and vary texture across the four categories.

anchors.role: Fixed elements are read from the photo and are never recolored.

split.dominant60: The largest area. Start from the wall colour. Textiles in this share stay close to it so the room still feels like itself.
split.secondary30: Sofa, rug and timber. This share carries the material weight: weave, jute, oak.
split.accent10: One idea only, usually a cushion, the art, or a throw edge. If the accent is loud, it stays in this share.

harmony.analogous: Accent hue stays within about 30 degrees of the timber hue, or slides toward the wall if the style is cooler. Use for calm, related schemes.
harmony.complementary: Accent sits near the opposite of the timber hue, then greyed down so it does not vibrate against the oak. Use sparingly.
harmony.monochrome: Accent is a deeper or lighter version of the same hue as the timber or the wall. Use when the style is about texture more than colour.

undertone.rule: Warm timber plus cool walls means the palette has to bridge them. Do not add an icy blue (it fights the oak) or a saturated orange (it fights the grey walls). Cool accents are greyed. Warm accents are softened with the wall colour.
undertone.bridge: Mix a little of the timber into a cool wall colour before using it as the 60 for a warm style. For a cool style, keep the wall and grey the accent.

texture.rule: Each style should use at least three texture families across cushions, rug, throw and art.

future: When a live photo is uploaded, sample the same four anchors and pass them through derivePalette in js/style-engine.js. Do not hard-code a new palette per photo.
